{"user":"I’m writing a literature review on how social media affects adolescent mental health. Can you propose a strong outline (section headings and what to include under each) for a 6–8 page paper, and suggest 6–8 key themes or categories I should cover?","plus_response":"Sure. Here’s a solid outline you can follow for a 6–8 page literature review, with section-by-section guidance—and I’ll also structure it so it can scale into a more ambitious, higher-quality version if you later expand the paper (e.g., adding clearer conceptual model + tighter synthesis across subfields):

1) Introduction (≈0.5–1 page)
- Briefly define the topic (social media use) and the outcome domain (adolescent mental health)
- State the review’s purpose and scope: what kinds of mental health outcomes (depression, anxiety, wellbeing, self-esteem, etc.) and what mechanisms/study types you cover
- Provide a one-paragraph roadmap of the rest of the paper

2) Conceptual Framework / Definitions (≈0.5–1 page)
- Define “social media exposure” in measurable terms (time spent, platform type, passive vs active use, social comparison, network size, algorithmic feeds)
- Define “mental health” outcomes and how studies operationalize them
- Optional but high value: a simple framework mapping exposure → mediators (e.g., comparison, cybervictimization) → outcomes

3) The Evidence Base: Study Designs and Measurement (≈1 page)
- Summarize common approaches: cross-sectional vs longitudinal vs experimental/quasi-experimental
- Discuss measurement issues: self-report bias, confounding (baseline mental health), time-varying effects
- Note what the literature can and cannot infer causally

4) Core Synthesis: Major Themes / Categories (≈2–3 pages)
Cover the themes below as subsections, each with: (a) what the theme claims, (b) what evidence supports/challenges it, and (c) typical limitations.

Suggested themes (use 6–8 of these, depending on your page budget):
- Passive consumption vs active engagement
- Social comparison processes (upward comparison, envy, appearance-related comparisons)
- Cyberbullying, harassment, and victimization
- Validation-seeking and feedback loops (likes, rewards, social reinforcement)
- Fear of missing out (FOMO) and stress/arousal pathways
- Identity development and self-presentation (benefits and risks)
- Moderators: gender, age, baseline mental health, personality traits
- Platform/environment differences (features, community norms)

5) Integrative Discussion (≈0.5–1 page)
- Reconcile conflicting findings: why studies diverge (measurement, confounders, heterogeneity)
- Identify which mechanisms have the strongest evidence
- Discuss practical implications cautiously (e.g., targeting mediators/contexts rather than “social media” broadly)

6) Research Gaps and Future Directions (≈0.5–1 page)
- Prioritize gaps by category: better longitudinal designs, consistent exposure measurement, moderator-focused studies
- Suggest what future studies should test (e.g., mediator models; differential effects by platform features)
- Close with a concise takeaway

If you want to push this to a more complex, higher-impact version, I can also:
- draft a one-paragraph synthesis for each theme (so you’re not just listing categories),
- propose a simple mediator-moderator diagram you can reference in multiple sections,
- and map a shortlist of candidate articles to each theme so you can write with a clear “who supports what” structure.","minus_response":"Here’s a workable outline you can use for a 6–8 page literature review, plus a set of themes.

1) Introduction
- Define social media use and adolescent mental health outcomes
- State what you’re reviewing and why it matters

2) How the Literature Measures Social Media and Mental Health
- Exposure (time, platform features, passive vs active)
- Outcomes (depression, anxiety, wellbeing, self-esteem, etc.)
- Study designs (cross-sectional vs longitudinal) and key measurement limits

3) Review of Findings by Theme (main body)
Use 6–8 subsections; for each one, summarize the general claim and then note inconsistencies/limitations.

Themes/categories to include:
- Passive vs active use
- Social comparison (upward comparison, appearance-related comparisons)
- Cyberbullying/harassment and victimization
- Validation/reward mechanisms (likes, feedback)
- FOMO/stress pathways
- Identity development and self-presentation (potential benefits/risks)
- Moderators (gender, baseline mental health, age, personality)
- Platform differences / community norms

4) Integrative Discussion
- Briefly reconcile mixed results (confounds, measurement issues, heterogeneity)
- Point out which mechanisms seem most supported

5) Gaps and Future Research
- What’s missing (e.g., stronger longitudinal/causal evidence, better exposure definitions)
- What would be ideal to test next

That outline should get you a complete structure; the rest is left as an exercise to you."}
